analysis.one_liner: Makes it illegal for meatpackers to buy rivals when the deal would leave the industry heavily concentrated.
analysis.headline: The bill to make meatpacking monopolies easier to block never got a hearing or a vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended a century-old law governing meatpackers so that any acquisition leaving the meat market too concentrated would automatically count as an illegal monopoly under the Clayton Act. It used a standard antitrust yardstick — the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index — with bright-line cutoffs, so regulators could block big meat-industry buyouts without proving each case in court. It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, who would benefit from more competition among meatpackers and potentially lower meat prices, and livestock farmers, who would face more buyers bidding for their cattle and hogs instead of a handful of dominant packers. Regulators would also gain a clearer legal standard for stopping consolidation before it happens.

how_it_helps.text: It would make any meatpacker acquisition that raised the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index above 1,800, or by more than 100 points, automatically illegal as a monopoly-creating merger and a Clayton Act violation [S2].
It gave the Justice Department and FTC a simple, bright-line test — instead of slow litigation over market shares — to stop big packers from buying rivals before consolidation happened [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpacking companies, which would face legal obstacles to acquiring competitors, and potentially their shareholders, since blocked acquisitions can limit growth.

drawbacks.text: The bright-line HHI test would flag mergers by formula rather than case-by-case analysis, which could block some acquisitions that would not actually raise prices — the kind of overreach antitrust skeptics typically object to.
It addressed future mergers only; it would not break up the concentration that already exists in meatpacking, so it would not by itself lower today's grocery or livestock prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real problem — a handful of meatpacking giants control most cattle and hog slaughter, and consumers and farmers both pay for that concentration. Its bright-line HHI test would have made blocking the worst mergers far easier than the current slow case-by-case approach. The cost is that a rigid numeric threshold could also block some mergers that would not actually hurt anyone, and the bill offered no exemptions for efficiency. On balance it was a modest, targeted consumer-and-farmer protection whose main weakness was that it never received any committee action or debate.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced it and sent it to the Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Hawley introduced the bill on September 14, 2023; the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day [S1].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote ever occurred [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died with it [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest meatpacking companies are better off: the merger and acquisition option that the bill would have closed remains open, and no new constraints were placed on the industry. Consumers and livestock farmers gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it read twice and referred to Judiciary.

for.name: 1 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as its only cosponsor from the other party.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for anyone to vote on it, and its lone cosponsor was a Democrat signing onto a Republican's bill, so the partisan shape was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would have barred big packers from acquiring rivals whenever a standard concentration measure would rise past fixed thresholds, blocking future consolidation. It died in committee, so their ability to keep acquiring is unchanged.
Fewer dominant buyers would mean more competition for their livestock and better prices. But because the bill never passed, they gained nothing; the buying power of the largest packers stands.
